newsitem.title: USA: Three former presidents back Clinton on China MFN.
newsitem.headline: Three former presidents back Clinton on China MFN.

text.p: Pressing its case to maintain China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trade status, the White House on Monday released letters of support from former presidents George Bush, Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter.

The letters, and similar expressions of support from six former secretaries of state and 10 former secretaries of defence also made public by the White House, were designed to sway Congress one day before it is due to vote on the issue.

While acknowledging the United States has differences with China, Republicans Bush and Ford and Democrat Carter argued that revoking MFN, which confers normal trade status on a country, was not in the U.S. national interest.

"Witholding MFN is not a sensible approach to resolving our differences," Bush wrote Clinton. "Quite the contrary, I am convinced that withholding MFN, or even conditioning its application to China, would be severely counterproductive."
Former secretaries of state George Shultz, Lawrence Eagleburger, Alexander Haig, James Baker, Henry Kissinger and Cyrus Vance made similar arguments.

"MFN revocation would effectively cut off trade between our two countries and thereby deal a devastating blow to our overall relationship," they wrote. "It would undermine the progress we have made working with China on critical issues, from stability on the Korean Peninsula to stemming the flow of illegal aliens and narcotics."
The White House released the letters in San Francisco, where Clinton is making a brief visit to speak to the annual conference of mayors and to raise funds for fellow Democrats.
Under U.S. law, the president each year must decide whether to grant China MFN and Congress has the right to disapprove his decision.

Some members of Congress have been reconsidering support for normal U.S. trade ties with China because of reports of human rights abuses, nuclear technology and missile transfers and allegations that Beijing tried to influence U.S. elections through illegal campaign contributions.

Ten former secretaries of defence -- Harold Brown, Dick Cheney, Melvin Laird, William Perry, Donald Rumsfeld, Frank Carlucci, Clark Clifford, Robert McNamara, Elliot Richardson and James Schlesinger -- made a similar plea.

"In our view, American interests are best served by a secure, stable and open China," they wrote to Clinton. "While we recognise there are several thorny and disturbing issues in this complicated relationship, nonetheless we believe the most promising way to reach the goal of a stable China is for the United States to continue to build a relationship of mutual engagement with China ...," they said.

House of Representatives Republican Leader Dick Armey announced last week that he would reluctantly support Clinton's MFN decision and support appeared to be growing among other lawmakers despite problems in the relationship.
The United States grants Most Favoured Nation trade status to almost every country in the world. Without it, tariffs on imported goods would soar to the high levels of the 1930's.
